Chapter 2: Rethinking What Counts as “Real” Cooking
There’s a quiet relief in realizing that real cooking doesn’t have to look like what you see on television or in those glossy magazines.
So many of us get caught up in this idea that cooking has a set of rules—like, you have to follow recipes to the letter, use only the freshest, most exotic ingredients, and somehow make every meal look like it belongs in a food ad.
But you know what? Most of the time, real life is way messier than that. Most folks are just trying to get something on the table before hunger tips over into frustration.
Picture a single parent, juggling work and kids, staring down a recipe that calls for a dozen ingredients—half of which she’s never even heard of. Just the thought of shopping, chopping, and cleaning up? That’s enough to make anyone close the cookbook and grab the phone for takeout.
But then, on a hectic night, she reaches for a bag of frozen veggies, tosses them in a pan with some leftover rice, adds a splash of soy sauce, and in ten minutes—dinner’s done. The kids eat without complaint, and for a moment, there’s this small, quiet sense of victory.
That kind of improvisation? It’s often brushed off as cheating, but honestly, it’s the heart of home cooking for most people.
Here’s something to pay attention to—shortcuts aren’t just okay, they’re often necessary. Frozen vegetables, pre-cooked grains, rotisserie chicken, jarred sauces, canned beans...these are the tools that keep dinner doable. If you look closely, you’ll see that the best home cooks are usually the ones who use these little tricks—no apologies needed.
There’s this myth that using convenience foods somehow makes you lazy or less of a cook. But in reality, it’s a smart way to get food on the table without adding stress to your day.
Think of a young professional, living on their own for the first time, discovering that a simple can of soup gets a major upgrade with a handful of spinach and a sprinkle of cheese. Is it fancy? Not really. But it’s fast, it’s nourishing, and it works.
Every small win like that builds confidence, and suddenly, the kitchen doesn’t feel so intimidating anymore.
The idea that every meal should be made from scratch? Honestly, that just keeps a lot of people from cooking at all.
The truth is, most folks who cook regularly are mixing fresh, frozen, and packaged ingredients all the time. What matters isn’t whether it’s “authentic” or “correct”—it’s whether it works for you. A sandwich, a quick bowl of pasta with jarred sauce, a salad from pre-washed greens...it all counts as cooking.
And here’s another thing: Cooking is a skill, not some magical talent you’re born with.
No one comes out of the womb knowing how to chop an onion or boil an egg. It’s something you learn—awkwardly at first, maybe, but it gets easier every time you try. The kitchen becomes a place for small experiments, not some high-stakes performance.
Imagine a group of friends gathering for a potluck. Some bring homemade dishes, others show up with a store-bought salad or maybe just a box of cookies. No one’s keeping score. What really matters is the simple act of sharing a meal together.
In those moments, it’s clear—the value of cooking isn’t about how complicated the dish is. It’s about the comfort and connection that comes from feeding yourself and others.
So, when you let go of those rigid ideas about what counts as “real” cooking, you open the door to a much more relaxed, forgiving approach.
It’s not about impressing anyone. It’s not about living up to some impossible standard. It’s about finding a way to feed yourself—and the people you care about—in a way that actually feels doable, even on the toughest days.
